utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. The registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution, examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're just trying to get the diagram lined up on the video, Your Honour. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bicic. Dobra dan. Yesterday we were discussing the TO, an incident which occurred approximately April 22nd to 24th, where several beatings occurred, and the day started where Omer Nalic was stabbed in the arm with a bayonet by Cera. Do you recall testifying about that yesterday, Mr. Bicic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you, with the pointer, please show on the diagram where Mr. Nalic was stabbed.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's right inside the detention room, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, inside the detention room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then you said they brought some people outside to the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you one more quick question about Mr. Nalic. What happened to his arm after he was stabbed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His arm was bleeding. Later on, when they stopped beating us and went away, we tried to stop the bleeding, but we didn't have any bandages, so we used a T-shirt. However, a day or two later, the arm became infected because the bayonet or the knife had been dirty or even smeared with lubricant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he ever receive any medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the following day, a nurse or someone like that came and cleaned the wound a little, but this wasn't enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long did it take for the arm to repair itself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a long time, because when they transferred us to Brcko, his arm was infected there. The wound was a bit infected. And they gave him some assistance there too, cleaning this and giving him some pills against blood poisoning or whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's go outside to the courtyard. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that Cera kicked or stepped -- what did he do to your brother's fingers to break them, three of your brother's fingers? Did he kick them, step on them, punch them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were beating my brother in this corner here between these storerooms, and my brother stumbled from the blows and fell to the floor, so that his left hand was on the concrete. Then Cera ran up and stomped on his hand with the heel of his military boot and broke three of his fingers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While this was happening to the four prisoners outside, what were the rest of the prisoners doing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest of the prisoners were standing in the room and singing the Chetnik songs they were ordered to sing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened after your brother's fingers were broken? What happened to the group of prisoners that were outside?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beating us and kicking us. They pushed us into the room, and then they took some other people out. I think one of them was Salkic, another one was Izetbegovic, and there were some others who had been inside, and the rest of us had to stand and sing the songs they made us sing. While I was singing those songs, when I saw my brother's hand, which was swelling rapidly, I gestured to the other detainees who were there with us, asking them to sing louder, and I took my brother's hand and pulled his fingers, crying all the time. We were both crying, my brother and I. He was crying from pain and I because I had to do this for him without any doctor nearby or any medical assistance. I managed to set two of his fingers more or less well, and the third finger is still not completely mobile. It healed the way it was broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At the Territorial Defence building, did your brother receive any medical attention for the three broken fingers on his left hand?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. We only had a nurse, who helped Omer Nalic, and she gave us some painkillers which he took to lessen pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's continue on that same day. Do you know a man by the name of Sejo Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Sejo Mujkanovic. He was a policeman in our town, and I had known him for about ten years. That's how long he had been a policeman. Maybe he had been a policeman longer. I say "about ten" because I'm not sure exactly how long it was. He was a policeman in the Bosanski Samac police station, and he was detained together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened to him on that day? Did Lugar do something to him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sead Mujkanovic was standing near Omer Nalic, in this area here, in this part of the building, in other words, opposite where my brother and I and the others who were with us were, somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you show the Court again? Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the Court get a chance to see? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the members of the Tribunal get a chance to see where he was identifying on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lugar came in. We continued standing and singing. Lugar came in and hit him with his rifle butt in the chest or in the head. I couldn't see exactly where he hit him because Lugar's body was between us. Sejo fell down onto the concrete floor of the room, then Lugar forced him to open his mouth very wide, and when he did, he put the barrel of his rifle and the sight which was near the end of the barrel, and then he pulled the rifle suddenly out of his mouth. And I could see that because his body had moved so he wasn't blocking my view any more. And in this manner, he pulled out several of his teeth. There was a dreadful scream from the policeman. And the other man continued. He kicked him with his booted feet. And then several other men who were standing around also received blows from him and then he went out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let us move to a day or two later. Do you know any -- did you ever meet any soldiers named Avram and Beli or "bel-I"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A day or two later, Avram and Beli came into the room. They forced us to sing. They beat some people using police truncheons. Then they took my brother outside. They closed the door behind them. We continued singing, but we could hear screams, and I recognised my brother's voice. They were beating him outside. Then they took him away somewhere; we didn't know where. He was absent for a few hours. I can't be certain how long it was because they had taken away our watches a few days previously. When my brother came back, he told us that they had held weapons pointed at his head, taken him to a house and down our street, and they forced my brother to ask neighbours and acquaintances for money so that they wouldn't kill me. In other words, they blackmailed him; they extorted money from him, to give them money to save my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us go to the next day, the day that you left. Let's begin in the morning, mid-morning hours, the arrival of Lugar. Could you tell us -- could you tell us what happened, beginning with the mid-morning hours?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 10.00, in our estimation, we heard -- because there was a kind of eerie silence, we heard the sound of our jeep motor. It stopped in front of the iron gate of the building, and we were all petrified. We were all paralysed by fear, my brother and I and the others, because we had grown familiar with the sound of that engine. Then the iron gate opened with a bang. We heard Lugar's voice, which we all knew well by now, and he ordered us to sing, cursing our mothers. We jumped to our feet, because we had been sitting on the concrete. We stood against the wall, and we started singing. At that point, a pistol shot rang out. The bullet pierced the metal door leading into our room - I can show you where - and it hit this wall between Dikan and Macak, who were standing and singing together with us. Then the metal door opened, and we saw -- we saw him standing there, Lugar. His face was all red. He was breathless. He looked terrible. He looked round the room. The door was still open. He went back to this spot here where one of the guards was sitting. His nickname was Sole, and he was from the surroundings of Samac. He was sitting on a wooden chair. Lugar smashed the chair with his foot. He broke it apart, and he grabbed a leg of the chair. It was about 80 or 90 centimetres long or perhaps a metre. He grabbed the back leg of the chair, and then he walked into the room carrying this chair leg. He hit Dikan, who was on his right-hand side. He hit him in the head. The man fell down or, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rather, he stumbled. He hit him in the head again, and then he fell down. About -- it was about in the middle of the room where there was a wooden beam or pillar holding up the ceiling, supporting the ceiling, and next to it was a white plastic container with water. That was our drinking water. The water container was open, and the water suddenly became red with Dikan's blood. After this, Lugar hit Osman Jasarevic. He hit him in the forehead. Osman fell to the ground. Then he called to Dasa, Mersad Gibic. He told him to approach him. Dasa approached him, and he hit him several times with this wooden object, which cracked, so he threw it away. And then he said, turning to me and my brother, "Brothers, go outside." He went before us, if I can show you, to this garage which was here. There was an old truck here, an old JNA truck. It was full of refuse, scraps, metal scraps. There was even a jack there, also a big metal bar which was about 2 and a half metres long and 8 to 10 centimetres thick, and this was used for towing trucks or military vehicles. We stood halfway between the garage and the room where we had been detained. Lugar took this bar from the truck. He was furious. He was fuming. The others had to continue singing. He grabbed this bar, raised it above his head, and circled around us, brandishing this metal rod over our heads. Then he told us, "I have orders to kill you." My brother and I were afraid. We were paralysed by fear when we saw his eyes and his expression and the metal rod that he was brandishing all around us. Then he told us that on that day was a big Serbian holiday, that it was Easter, and he said to us, "Look what I have to do instead of celebrating. I have to kill." I don't know how my brother and I looked at that moment, but I think our legs were giving way. We just stood there silently and looked at him. After this, he asked the guard, "Is the Ustasha moving?" He was, of course, referring to Dikan, who had remained on the floor in the room, the detention room. He said he was moving his legs. Then he threw the metal rod against the garage wall. We continued standing there. We didn't move. We saw him go into the room, grab Dikan by the collar and pull him to the door of the room, where he simply left him. I can show you. It was here. His head was in the direction of the water pump which was in the middle of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please show us again on the diagram.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, through the door. His head was in the direction of the water pump.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happens next?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was on his way back towards us, he told us to move a little to one side. So we moved aside for about a metre, and he circled us nervously, looking at us all the time, or rather, looking at the place where he had left Dikan. At one point he was halfway facing us and Dikan, and then, quite simply, he pulled a pistol from under his sweatshirt. He pointed it a little at me, a little at my brother, and continued circling us, pointing the gun now at one, now at the other. As I have already said, we were terrified, and we kept waiting for the pistol to go off. We expected to be shot. However, when he had his back turned to Dikan, he suddenly swung round and shot in Dikan's direction. Although I was in a state of shock because of everything that was going on, I saw the body move. Then he fired another shot, and I saw the man's head burst open. I saw a piece of his brain and pieces of his skull spatter around. This was so horrible that we were aghast, even though we didn't dare move from the place he had told us to stand in. Then somebody from the police station which was across the street - I don't know who it was - called out to Lugar and said, "Come here. The coffee is ready." He approached us and said, "These Serbs have a lot against you, but some of them say you are good people, so this time I won't kill you." Then he turned to the guard and said, "Bring a truck and throw this trash into the River Sava." He was referring to Dikan. He left through the iron gate and went off in the direction of the police station. When the truck drove into the yard, the guard told us to put Dikan's body onto the back of the truck, but my brother and I asked him to excuse us, because we could barely stand up the way we felt, and I think we would not have been able to lift the body and load it onto the truck. The guard said, "All right." He took us back inside, and he took two younger men who were detained with us, and they put Dikan's body onto the truck. Then they came back. The door of the detention room was closed. There was a bullet hole left in it. It was right in the middle of the door approximately. We were all left speechless. I think we were all so terrified in that room that there was complete silence. For a certain length of the time nobody spoke. We just looked at one another. We were thinking of who would be next and when it would happen again. That afternoon, the same guard who had driven off the truck, who was there with us, told us that the special unit from Serbia had gone out into the field somewhere and that most probably we would be transferred to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll just stop you right there. The week -- the little over a week that you had spent at the TO, which is just prior to the transfer of Brcko, during that period, were you able to bathe?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not once were we able to bathe or wash ourselves. I can show that mostly in the evening, they let us relieve ourselves in the area of the yard, in all of the yard, or in the one toilet that was in the Territorial Defence building. They would take us in through this door, through a room to the toilet, which was under the staircase leading upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about your clothes? Were you able to wash your clothes or get new clothes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We continued sitting there in the same clothes we had been brought in in from our homes. We were all in bloodstained and dirty clothing. We had no change of clothes, so the blood and the dirt from the beatings remained. There was nothing we could do to remove it. We didn't have any water, so we could neither wash our clothes nor change.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we describe your meals? Were you fed well? Were you fed enough food?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times in the afternoon they put us onto the truck and drove us to a factory which had a kitchen. There we would eat mostly leftovers after the Serbian army and police, who probably ate there. We would spend an hour or an hour and a half there, and we would get something like a cooked meal, maybe consisting of several sorts of dishes all thrown together into one pot. So we ate that. And in the evening, one of the local Serbs who were able to come to us would bring us a can, a tin, so that those of us who were able to eat would eat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were people hungry?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were probably hungry, but nobody really cared for food because of all the suffering. Everybody was thinking about whether he would perhaps be the next to die in this cruel way or whether he would perhaps be the next to be beaten. So at that time, food meant nothing to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were prisoners ever beaten after the meals?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already said that there were no rules in this, so it didn't matter whether it was morning, afternoon, evening, or night. They would simply come in and vent their rage on us whenever they had an opportunity to do this. They would come at any time, by day or by night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On the eve of the move to Brcko, what was the condition of you, your brother Hasan, and the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were so humiliated, so battered that we could barely move. Our faces were all swollen. We all had bruises on our bodies. We were all broken, so that we looked very, very pitiful indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's go to the transfer. Can you tell the members of the Chamber what happened on that evening, as best you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that evening, Mr. Topolovac, who was my neighbour and who had been the commander of the police station in our town for a few years back, and two or three other men - I can't remember who else was there - they visited us. They brought two military trucks into the yard of the Territorial Defence. These trucks had belonged to the JNA, and I think they still belonged to the JNA, but I can't be sure. They called out our names, and we boarded the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the defendants being there calling out names or taking any part in this transfer?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I know only that Mr. Topolovac stood there. I even talked to him briefly. He said to me, "Neighbour, you're going to Brcko. You'll probably be safer there than you are here." That's all I was able to find out. But I was in such a sorry state that day, after the murder of Dikan and after my brother and I had been taken into the yard where we had undergone such an ordeal, and were in a state of shock when we had been told that orders had been given that we should be killed, so I was still suffering from the consequences of this, and I was afraid of this transfer. I wasn't sure they were taking us where my neighbour had said they were. So I can't remember. I can't remember any names or any other people at the present time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happens? Do you get on the trucks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called out names from that list one by one, and we got onto the truck. We were all there, those of us whose names had been called out previously. We didn't know immediately that several people had been left behind in those rooms where we had all been detained. They closed the trucks with canvas. They told us not to try to run away because -- I don't know what it's called, but a personnel carrier or something like that with a big machine-gun was escorting us, and so were some cars. In the dark, we couldn't see very well what kind of vehicles they were, but we heard behind us very loud engines, so it must have been something like a personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was it a long ride?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my estimation, or the estimation of several of us, it was quite long. I can't say exactly how long, because I'm not sure, but probably because of the state I was in, I wouldn't be able to really determine how long it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually arrive somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was dark. We stopped in front of a building. Then they took us off the trucks. We saw that there were people wearing JNA uniforms. They took us off the trucks one by one and they took us into the building. There was a sort of entrance hall in the building. They pushed each of us against the wall, searched us, collected all our documents, money, if anyone had any left in their pockets or hidden somewhere on their person, in their filthy clothing. If anyone had a driving licence or an identity card or any kind of document, all this was confiscated. Then they tied our hands behind our backs with a piece of string and they pushed us into a room which had only iron bars for a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. door. I don't know how many of us they crammed into this tiny cell, but we were packed in like sardines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long -- first, actually, before that: Do you know in which municipality you were?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not long afterwards a young lieutenant arrived. He was the one who had come while I was at the police station. Mr. Salkic recognised him. He had gone with him with an escort of soldiers who were subordinate to that lieutenant to collect weapons from people who had weapons in the town of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did he --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear to us then, and this lieutenant actually told us, that we were in the JNA barracks in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at those JNA barracks in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed there until the 2nd of May, when there was shooting in the town, in other words, when war broke out there also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was anyone beaten while you were being held at those barracks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not as brutally, not nearly as badly as we were beaten in the previous detention in the Territorial Defence or in the police station right after we were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was anyone from Bosanski Samac, any of the Bosanski Samac prisoners, beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the prisoners from Bosanski Samac, several of them were beaten, but as I say, it wasn't nearly as bad as what had happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was anyone forced to sing Chetnik songs or Serbian patriotic songs, or sing anything?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then a gentleman who arrived wearing civilian clothes - and later on we learned that he was a major in those barracks - he asked us what we had been singing. We told him, and we even started singing those Chetnik songs. Then he stopped us, and he asked us whether we knew the Yugoslav anthem. In contrast to the songs we had sung previously, we sang this in unison, I could almost say in one breath, and we were all surprised. After this visit, some people complained that their hands were tied too tightly with the string, so they loosened the string, in some cases; in some cases, they untied it completely. And as for myself, I waited for morning and then I asked for my hands to be untied, because my wrists were very painful and my hands were numb tied behind my back like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you ever interrogated? Were you, your brother, or anyone else interrogated while at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember what day it was. We were taken to the neighbouring building. We went there one by one. I, myself, was

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: going on and why we had been brought there. Of course, under such conditions, my nerves were giving way, and so I shed a few tears. After we had made a statement, we were taken to another room in that building, and we learned that this was the prison in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just stop there. How many people interrogated you during this interrogation session?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that room, there was Mr. Zaric; there was Mr. Jovo Savic, who before the war had worked in the neighbouring town of Orasje, also in the police station; and I can't remember who else was there. There was someone typing out our statements on a typewriter. There were the two of them, but it was Mr. Zaric who actually interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How were you treated during the interview? Did anyone harm you during the interview?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During the interview, no one beat us. No one even threatened us. It was an open and simple communication. We simply made a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What was your physical and mental state during the interview?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very hard for me. I felt so humiliated. I was so badly beaten up that, as I said, I even started to cry at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did anyone ask you what happened to you, why are you bloodied, beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How long had you known Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had known Simo Zaric for quite a long time, since the days when he went to secondary school in Bosanski Samac. He lodged with my relatives not far from my house. It was about 50 or 70 metres away from my house. At that time, he went to school together with a relative of mine. It was the economic vocational secondary school, together with Muharem Barjaktarevic, with whom he lodged. And I often kept company with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did he -- did he inquire during this interview about your physical condition?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't inquire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How long did this interrogation last, as best as you can determine?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately about half an hour, maybe a little longer. I can't say. It was a long time ago, nine and a half years ago, so I can't be certain as to how long it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did anyone complete typing the statement while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you get a chance to read it prior to signing it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in such a state that even had I read it, I probably wouldn't have understood it, because as I have already told you, I even started to cry, which means that perhaps I glanced through it and just signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you ask Simo for help? You'd known him for many years. He's known you for many years. He didn't inquire about your health, but did you ask him for any help?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one point when I started to cry, I asked him if he could help my brother and me and all of us. I think we were all innocent people locked up and tortured so brutally, without knowing the real reason why we had been brought there and tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And how did he answer you, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he answered with another question. He asked if we wanted to go back to our homes in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And did you respond?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, "Yes. If I will be free there, then I do want to go back to my home," or as there was no war yet, in a town where we had relatives. I asked if he could let us go to our relatives' house and we would manage somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think I received any reply that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did he or anyone at Brcko tell you why you and all these other civilians were being held?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during your stay in Brcko, approximately a week or so, were you allowed to bathe?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once they took us all together to the soldiers' bathroom. We went in single file with our hand on our heads. There we bathed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Okay. What about food? Were you provided with adequate food?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Brcko we were given some food, but I think that again these were leftovers, left over from the dinner or lunch of the soldiers who were in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Was it sufficient? Were people still hungry?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In most cases it was too little to satisfy the hunger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were you beaten during your stay in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Or, rather, it was shoving rather than beating, when we were brought in, pushed against the wall, when we were searched. But seeing the state I was in, I was so bloodied and swollen, I think those people didn't feel like beating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Other than the prisoners from Bosanski Samac, was anyone else being held in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We found a man there whom we later got to know. And during our stay there, they brought in two brothers from the Brcko area. They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And how were they treated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evening they brought them in, they beat them until morning. We could hear the groans of those people who were begging for mercy, asking not to be beaten so badly. But this went on from late at night until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: You indicated you were eventually transferred on or about May 2nd from Brcko. Could you describe how you were transferred?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bus came. We could hear shots and detonations, strong explosions outside. We were told to go in single file and board the bus, in which there were curtains drawn over the windows. We had to put our heads down. And that's how they drove us somewhere. We didn't know in what direction we were going or where they were taking us to, because we had no opportunity to look out of the window or to raise our heads above the seats, the backs of the seats. So we drove along bending forward, and we were not allowed to raise our heads and look around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were you eventually brought somewhere, and did you learn where you were?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They brought us to the JNA barracks in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: No. You had just left Brcko. Where did you go from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I was a little confused. They brought us to the barracks in Bijeljina, and there there was an open space where soldiers were lining up, and there was a bust there of Jahic, known as Spanac, who had been a World War II hero.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the barracks in Bijeljina, did everyone get off at once or what sort of procedure did they have, did they use to remove everyone from the bus?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We dismounted one by one, with our hands on our heads, with our heads down. We passed through a line of soldiers. They separated off a man whom they had put on the bus together with us in Brcko. They beat him. We could see as we were passing, several metres away from us, that they were beating him. And finally, someone said, "Why are you beating him? Kill him." Not far away from there, as we were being taken into the building, we heard the sound of automatic gunfire and a scream, and I looked round and saw the man falling - I don't know who he was or what his name was - and I think there are several other people who saw this and who can testify to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did they kill him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they killed him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did they bring you inside the building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they brought us inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And where did they bring you in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Where did they bring you in the building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken upstairs. I don't know whether it was the first or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. second floor. There they put us in a room, quite large room. They told us to face the wall and then to kneel down. They said we were not to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did anything happen if you moved?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone moved, some soldiers would immediately come from behind him and start beating him all over, on his head, neck, back. I don't know for how long we knelt there like that, but our legs went numb - all of us felt this - so that each one of us simply had to move a little, and whoever moved would get a blow on the back or head or neck with a truncheon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you stay there for the whole evening, or did they bring you somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this, we had again to put our hands on our heads and trot, if we could, because our legs were completely numb. But we had to, because along the way we would get blows from rifle butts or truncheons held by the soldiers who were around us. And in this way, we were taken to the gym, or sports hall, which was in the barracks compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Bijeljina at the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed in Bijeljina in that sports hall until the 13th of May, when the same policemen who had guarded us in Brcko and brought us to the barracks in Bijeljina arrived with a bus and his escort and took us to Brcko and then in the direction of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's stay -- move back for a while. While you were there, Bijeljina, were you or any of the prisoners beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion when we were kneeling again, facing the wall, we had to bend our heads down toward our knees as far as we could. I received a terrible blow in the area of my right kidney. It was, in fact, a kick from a foot in a military boot, and it was so hard that it lifted me off the ground. I moaned and fell. After this, the same thing happened to Salkic, my brother, and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you suffer any injuries as a result of this kick with a boot?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After this there was blood in my urine for days, and an officer of the Serbian army, or the JNA, even spared Ibela and me, because Ibela was also urinating blood. I'm referring to Mr. Salkic. This officer ordered the military policemen - who were wearing white belts, which was the distinguishing mark of a military policeman - the officer ordered them that no one was to beat us, me and Mr. Salkic. We were not given any medical assistance, but for a few days we lay on the parquet floor of the sports hall and we were even given a blanket. It was a military blanket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Could you describe the hygiene in Bijeljina during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a few days in Bijeljina in the sports hall, which had a bathroom, we were allowed to take a bath there. A military policeman brought us a razor - one or two razors. I can't remember exactly - so we all shaved with it. We were pulling the hair out of our cheeks rather than shaving it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's 11.00, Counsel. We shall have our break and continue the proceedings at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Examination-in-chief is continuing with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Bicic, we were talking about Bijeljina. One last question about that location: Could you describe the meals and the food that you received?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received two meals a day while we were there, more in the afternoon; that is to say, after the regular dinner being prepared for the soldiers in the barracks, we would get what was left over. But we got more food. The quantity was bigger than in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Was it sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, compared to what it was like before, it was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you left that location at some time. You indicated you returned to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that you left or approximate date?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 13th of May. That's when we heard from the military policemen in Bijeljina that at one time, the 13th of May in the former Yugoslavia was policemen's day. It was celebrated as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And how were you transported? Tell the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They put us back on the buses the same way, with an escort, the same escort that escorted us from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us via Brcko in the direction of Obudovac, or rather, Samac. In Obudovac, they changed places and some other soldiers got on, and they accompanied us to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Where do you go when you arrive in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We first stopped by the textile factory, and those soldiers showed us the barracks. They indicated the Serb army barracks in the factory itself. We stopped there for a brief period of time, and then they drove us off towards the police station in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you stop at the police station?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not far from the police station, that's where the bus stopped, and we stayed there for some time. We did not get out. I don't know why we were waiting, but soon afterwards, they took us off again in the direction of the secondary school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Do you eventually arrive at some location?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived in the yard of the secondary school centre, by the gymnasium of that same school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber what happens upon arrival.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They opened the doors of the bus, and we got out in a column, once again with our hands on our heads. We got off the bus one by one and had to run the gauntlet; that is to say, there were two lines, one line on each side of people in uniforms, policemen wearing police uniforms and camouflage uniforms, and they beat us with their weapons. They kicked us with their feet while we were passing by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were you struck?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They struck us with the weapons that they had, usually rifles, and kicked us with their boots, army boots which they had on their feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did a firearm go off at any time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one particular moment, one of the policemen hit my brother who was in front of me, and his rifle let out a shot. Several bullets, in fact, were fired, and one of them ended up lodged in the bus. It hit the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, these people who were beating you, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they were from Bosanski Samac and the surrounding parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were these soldiers or police officers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Some of them were wearing police uniforms and the others were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, after everyone was beaten exiting the bus, where did they bring you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us in through a hallway and changing room belonging to the gym of the secondary school centre and lined us up against the wall, and more than half the wall was brick, and above -- half of the wall was brick and the other half was glass, thick, a thick layer of glass, so that light came into the hall through the glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Was anyone beaten at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They beat Kemal Atic. One of the policemen brought a wooden rod with a nail or screw, with a screw on it, and I noticed later on that this wooden rod had been pulled away from one of the ladders for gymnastics that was fixed to the wall of the hall. He took out a man who had joined us, whom they had captured in Brcko, or rather, imprisoned in Brcko, and then he brought me out and ordered me to use that rod to beat that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did anything else happen? Was there any shooting? Was there any other beatings? Did anything else occur?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I went back to my place underneath the glass bricks - they were, in fact - some other people in uniform turned up and they provoked us. They spat at us. Some of them shot at that glass that was above our heads, and the shattered fragments fell on us and on the floor of the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: On that first day that you were at the secondary school, did you see any of the defendants visiting that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I saw any of the defendants that day, but the following day a larger group came, with Stevan Todorovic and Mr. Blagoje Simic, a man who was very big and fat, and they called him "Fatty." I heard them do that. They looked around the hall, looked at us, and then I heard Mr. Blagoje Simic say, "There's enough room here." After that, they left the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were more prisoners brought in at any later time or in a recent time to that statement that "There's more room here"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that same day when we were put up in that building, another group was brought in, towards evening. I don't know how many of them, but they were people who had been brought from their homes that day. They were told they would be going for interviews, interrogations, but they joined them onto us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of these people who were being held at the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that, for the most part -- or rather, half of us were Muslims and the other half were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were these prisoners soldiers or military personnel or were they wearing military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were all civilians, wearing our civilian clothing, suits and suchlike.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we stayed there for two nights. We slept there for two nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then they told us that we should form a column and go one -- proceed one by one with our hands on our heads and that we should go outside. When we went outside, they made us run across several playing fields which were located between the secondary school centre itself and the primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And then where did they bring you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then they put us up in the gym hall belonging to the primary school this time, which was the only one that had remained intact, because all the other buildings belonging to the school had been set fire to and had been -- were semi-destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have another diagram. Mr. Zecevic provided an architectural-type diagram of the primary school for all counsel to use. I have already provided it with the registrar. Could the usher -- could we have it marked, please, for identification, and then Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could the usher place them in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you wish it to be part of the evidence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At this time just to be marked for identification, to be used as a diagram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked P30 ter ID, P30 ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, do you recognise this document that's been placed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it, but I think that something is lacking. There was another space, another area here which was in between the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just show us where that is for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another small space here like a workshop which the caretaker used, and there was another little wall here with a door here. So first you went into this small hallway to the left. That is to say, this was the workshop, the caretaker's workshop; the person who maintained the central heating, which was here. It was the boiler room, actually, for the central heating system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: However, sir, is this sufficient to be used as an aid during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should just like to indicate that this wall here was a brick wall halfway up, and then above that were glass panes, windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Could you show us -- where were you held while at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were held here, in this gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long were you held there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about -- that is to say, from mid-May to the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, during that time, did you get to meet a person named Debeli?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet that individual, who came frequently with Stevo Todorovic, and I saw him personally for the first time in the company of Stevo Todorovic and Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Was he a large or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: "Debeli" was "Fatty."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a very big, fat man, quite a bit taller than me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, when he came --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and fatter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, when he came, what did he have you do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were forced - like we were previously when we were held in the Territorial Defence building - to sing Chetnik songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: In addition to the Chetnik or the Serbian patriotic songs, did you have to chant anything, any slogans or any chants?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were forced to do that. We were forced to say, "Serbia will stretch to Tokyo. Wherever there are Serbs living, it is Serb land."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And did you have to do that every time Debeli and Todorovic visited?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, how often would Stevan Todorovic visit?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And did he come during the day or in the night or in the early morning hours? When did he come?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would come unexpectedly, at any time of the day or night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And were there beatings when he came?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every time they would beat the people in the hall. They would take some of them out into the corridor in front of the gym hall as well, but mostly we were beaten inside, in the gym, when Stevan Todorovic came by.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did he use any implements to do these beatings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was always escorted by seven or eight or even as many as ten other men who would come in. They were his escorts, and they would bring with them various wooden objects, among others, a baseball bat, and they would use it to beat us. They would beat us, and very often, Todorovic would beat us too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were you ever beaten by Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He beat me several times, and my brother as well, also several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a man by the name of Silvestar Antunovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Silvestar Antunovic. He was a policeman before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Was he a prisoner at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was incarcerated together with us, and his place was next to me, on my right-hand side. He would either lie down or stand, but he was always there, Mr. Antunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you have certain places in the gym where you were forced to sit or sleep or stand?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we arrived, they would position us. The soldiers lined us up when they escorted us into the hall and said that we weren't to change our places, that we had to stick to those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Using the diagram, do you recall or could you show the Court where your place was in that gym?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly here. As you go in to the right, next to the right-hand wall, 2 or 3 metres from the corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And where was your brother, Hasan, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in front of me. Salkic was in front of my brother. In front of Salkic was Buco. Hadzialijagic was in front of Buco, and in front of him there was Dragan Delic. And just behind the door here was Omer Nalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Do you recall where Silvestar Antunovic sat?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did something happen to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And for the record, Counsel, you simply say that the witness indicated the seatings of the prisoners inside the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you like me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that's all. That's okay. Yes. Just you remember the next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Silvestar Antunovic, did something happen to him while at the primary school? Could you tell the Chamber what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one night - it was late into the night - we heard the sounds of several cars stopping in front of the building where the gym hall was. We knew that we were in for an unpleasant visit. Not long after that, the guards shouted at us and told us to sing. They in fact ordered us to sing. And then about ten soldiers came into the hall, wearing camouflage uniforms, together with Stevan Todorovic. While we were singing and shouting "Serbia stretching to Tokyo," Stevan Todorovic would use a strong flashlight and beam it in our faces, beaming this light into our eyes, and in this way he would select victims on whom he would take it out on. Then he would beat us. He would beat us personally, while his escorts would be beating others. That particular night, the beating, as I saw it, and according to the others, lasted for a whole eternity. Once Todorovic flashed his flashlight into Silvestar Antunovic's eyes, who was standing next to me while I was singing, and all the others as well, and he proceeded to beat him with the baseball bat. He beat him on his head and on his body. And when he started to fall down, they would pull him up, the guards or the soldiers who had come together with Todorovic. Then Todorovic would move on to someone else, while the rest of us were beaten by his guards, so that he would make the rounds and go right round the hall that we were put up in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Was Esad Cosic in the room that evening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Esad Cosic is his name. He sat somewhere in this area here, in this part of the hall, which means that we were lined up right around these walls. This area here in the middle was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just one second. Your Honour, for the record, Esad Cosic was identified as sitting towards the top left-hand corner of the gym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What happened to Esad Cosic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw, from the side we were on, Stevan Todorovic flashing the flashlight into him, and he clearly indicated -- it was clear that it was Stevan Todorovic, and he hit the man with the baseball bat several times on the body and on his head. Esad Cosic fell down. I think he lost consciousness. Todorovic's escorts kept on beating him for a little while while he was lying down, forcing him to get up, but the man just couldn't get up. He would go back to the circle or go back the way he came, left me and Silvestar the way he had approached us, and went away from us and my brother and all the rest, and he personally beat people. I think he hit everyone at least once or several times with that baseball bat, practically everyone. When he got back to where Silvestar was - and in the meantime, the soldiers had managed to pick him up and Silvestar had regained consciousness slightly - he hit him several times again with that baseball bat. The man fell down without a sound coming from him, and he made no movement. Then he started beating me and my brother, and Salkic as well, and he kicked us with his legs and beat us with the bat, swearing at us, cursing us all the while. They said -- he said, "Where are your cars, you proprietors?" Not long after that, he would move on to others, and even to his friend, Omer Nalic. He would often sit with him in our pizzeria. When I say "often," I mean several times a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did they eventually leave that evening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, after he had beaten Omer Nalic, Omer, semi-conscious as he was, because he had received several blows to his head as well, said that he would complain and that he would look for Chief Todorovic. Probably he had lost control of his faculties and didn't realise that Todorovic himself was the man who had just beaten him up. After that, they left the hall. The others, of course, throughout this time, had to keep singing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What was the condition of the prisoners after they left?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they left, the people who had been beaten less, who had received fewer blows in those beatings from the guards - that is, the guards took them out to bring some water and clean up the place, clean the blood from the floor of the hall; it was a plastic floor covering - so that those of us who were bleeding were able to wash at least a little of the blood off our faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What was the condition of Silvestar Antunovic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Silvestar Antunovic did not regain consciousness the whole night, although we kept washing him, pouring water over him. So until morning, until it became light and we were able to see him properly, he continued to lie in this sort of coma. He was alive but in a sort of coma. Esad Cosic, also on that morning, asked to be taken to the toilet, because he was conscious. However, when he took a step, his right leg quite simply went up in the air, that he was unable to control it. He wasn't able to take a step normally or to stand on his right leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were released -- or you were exchanged in September?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: In early September, when you were exchanged, was Esad Cosic still with you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And what was the condition of his leg two, three months later, in September?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the same state as it had been on that morning. Two of us who were incarcerated always had to take him out to the toilet or to help him when he had to walk, because, quite simply, the man wasn't able to control the movement in his right leg or to put his weight on that leg, to stand on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What happened to Silvestar Antunovic? Did he ever regain consciousness?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, following the night when we were beaten, we asked the guards to call a doctor to render medical assistance to Silvestar and to Cosic and also to the others who had been beaten. Sometime during the afternoon, a lady doctor came. Her name was Ruza, and she was a doctor in our town. She was accompanied by a nurse. She took a look at Cosic and at Silvestar and gave us some tablets, painkillers that she had with her. She asked the guards that Silvestar and Cosic should be taken to hospital; however, they took Silvestar away, but Cosic stayed with us. I don't know where they took him. I didn't know at the time, but when I was exchanged, I learnt that Silvestar was taken to the hospital in Brcko and that from there he was transferred for treatment to the hospital in Belgrade, and from there - I don't know how - after he had recuperated, recovered, he succeeded in leaving those parts of Serbia and he returned to the territory of the Orasje municipality, which was not occupied at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What about Esad Cosic? Have you ever learnt the status of his leg?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not. I never talked to him afterwards, after I was exchanged, nor did I ever see him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: When you last saw him, he had no control of one of his legs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The last time I saw him, he had no control over his right leg. When he took a step -- if I can demonstrate this with my hand. When he wanted to make a normal step, his leg would shoot up to the level of his head. And as I knew him from before, and he said this himself, he said that never in his life was he able to lift his leg that high before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you know a man by the name of Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: During the middle part of June of 1992, did you ever see Milan Simic, the defendant Milan Simic, at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One evening - I think it was, I would say, about midnight - in that gym hall in which we were all put up, following orders from guards and some soldiers to get up on our two feet and to sing songs again, the songs that we had to sing, the Chetnik songs, as we were doing this, Mr. Simic came into the hall, accompanied by six or more other men. He called out the names of several of us. He ordered us to step out. And in the meantime, his escorts, like all the other escorts before this one, beat the people and us too while we were going out, and he called out the names. He called out my brother by name, as well as Perica Misic and Ibrahim Salkic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: You indicated that you were beaten as you exited the gym hall. What were you beaten with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They beat us, as far as I was able to notice, with the rifles that they held and with some firm objects, hard objects that they had in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were you struck, Mr. Bicic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. They struck me on my back, hurrying me up to go outside as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: So you leave the gym. What happens next?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went through the corridor. We were pushed out of it and beaten out. If I can demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went through this passageway here. They pushed us out here and lined us up along this wall, and as I said, above the second half of the wall were windows with glass panes. This is where there were several soldiers standing around. They were Mr. Simic's escorts, in fact. They beat us. Mr. Simic himself was standing somewhere here by the entrance. He was swearing at us and cursing us, using derogatory terms, insulting us, insulting the Muslims and the Croats. Perica Misic was a Croat. He was a man who for several years before the war was the -- had been the head of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, the witness pointed to the diagram and showed the movement from the gym, into the corridor, and lined them up into the entrance hall at the wall along the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: You're in that entrance hall, sir. Did the defendant Simic, Milan Simic, have anything in his hands?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simic had an automatic rifle -- pistol, sorry, a Scorpion. That was the pistol's name. And he waved it around in different directions. He turned it towards us, pointing it at us, and he shot several bullets. Luckily, the pistol had not been transferred to -- so that it could do a burst of gunfire, but it was individual gunshots, between the heads of me and my brother. And the glass partition that was behind our back shattered and the fragments fell all over us. After that, the soldiers beat us again. Someone gave orders that we should place -- put our hands up behind our necks or behind our heads and that we should spread our legs and stand that way. And then Mr. Simic aimed his boot at us. He aimed at our genitals, while the others were saying, "Serves them right. Serves the balijas right. It will prevent them from making any more children." These -- it was quite normal that we doubled up from the impact of the blows, and then we would be hit again on the back. They used various metal objects that were found thereabouts. If I may show you. It was in this part of the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in this area here, this part of the hallway, and they were the remnants of desks, schoolroom desks and chairs. And in the fire, when the school was set on fire, they were probably -- they had probably burnt down, the wooden parts. So there were a lot of these chair legs that remained and the legs of the children's desks. And because they probably didn't have enough police batons because they had broken them on us, then these other objects were used. They were new implements to wield and to beat us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Simic strike you or your brother with any object?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that one of his escorts handed him one of those bars, so that he had his pistol, automatic pistol, in one hand and the rod or bar in the other. So that when he struck us in our genitals, when he kicked us in our genitals with his boot, when we crouched down and doubled up, he would then proceed to hit us with that bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How was he dressed during this incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just one minute. If I can seek a clarification. Mr. Bicic, you used the word "we" several times. "We were struck in the genitals." Can you please identify the persons to whom this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. It was myself and my brother, as well as Perica Misic and Ibrahim Salkic. So we all had to stand with our legs wide apart so that Mr. Simic could select his victim and beat each one of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How was the defendant Simic, Milan Simic, dressed during this beating?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Simic was wearing a camouflage uniform on that occasion. Because it was summertime, he had trousers and a shirt on, and on his feet he had army boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, could you please stand up and show us how you had to stand against the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Would you please stand up and demonstrate how you had to stand against the wall prior to being kicked.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly in this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Your Honour, may the record reflect that the witness stood with his feet separated apart, say, roughly two feet - in North American, I'd say two-thirds of a metre - and that he had his hands behind his neck and that they were -- the fingers were crossed behind his neck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you were kicked, did he succeed in kicking you in the groin area, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but luckily, he hit me slightly above my sex organs. That's what happened to me. So that until I was exchanged, until the end, up above my sex organ I had a swelling, as big as a fist, I would say, and it caused me a great deal of pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What was the force of that kick?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The force? Well, if somebody is standing 2 metres away from you, takes two or three steps in a sort of semi-running stance and then aims, like a football player when he wants to hit the ball as hard as he can, when he takes aim and takes a swing, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: As a result of that kick, did you have any or did you suffer any physical problems?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe them.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to urinate, along with great pain, it would last longer. I was able to urinate but, as all the ducts had been clogged up from the blow, once a day, so that the quantity of urine which I was not able to release made the pain even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How long did this swelling and this urination problem last? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted until I was released, when I went to see a doctor. And I consulted my friends, and they took me to a specialist for those problems, and he helped me by giving me some tablets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did they explain what kind of problem you were suffering?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They said that this swelling was blocking some ducts. This swelling was simply pressing against them so that urine could not flow through normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: After your exchange, how many months was it before you healed from these injuries, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After, I think, about 20 days or a month, the swelling slowly subsided and disappeared, and then I was able to urinate with less pain, and the situation improved with time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How many times, sir, were you kicked in the area of the groin by Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, two or three times. In other words, more than once I was kicked, and then after that I was struck again several times with the rod or the pistol he was holding. The blow made me bend forward and then I would feel severe pain in my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: After this beating, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this beating, Mr. Simic's escort took us back to the room, hitting us all the time -- or rather, to the gym, and there the other detainees were singing without stopping. After this, they left and the other people tried to help us in any way they could, by soaking some old T-shirts in water and putting them on our swellings, on our back, and, in my case, below the stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see the defendant Milan Simic again?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About seven days later - I say "about" because I'm not sure whether it was five days or seven days or perhaps eight - we were ordered to sing again. We sang. It was night-time. Mr. Simic called out Perica Misic and my brother and took them away somewhere. We heard the car door closing. There were several doors closing. We don't know how many cars there were outside. We heard engines igniting and we heard the vehicles driving off away from the gym where we were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Who ordered you to sing? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards who were guarding us ordered us to sing, and I don't know who ordered them to tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, how long was your brother and Perica Misic away?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When dawn broke - and this was summertime, so dawn broke very early - my brother and Perica came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did they have anything with them when they came back, anything in their hands?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They brought us several cartons of cigarettes. There were a few dozen packets of cigarettes, which they distributed to all of us. My friend Salkic and I and the other people were very worried because the night passed so slowly for us, we didn't know where my brother had been taken and with what intention he had been taken away. When he returned, however, he distributed the cigarettes throughout the gym. Almost everybody who was a smoker received a packet of cigarettes. Then my brother sat down in his place next to me, Perica went back to his place. Of course the other detainees gathered around us asking questions about what had happened, asking where they had got the cigarettes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Let's move on a bit. Towards the end of June, do you recall being brought to the police station for an interview, to be interrogated by Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And was that you and your brother that were brought?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One day, two uniformed men arrived - they had police uniforms - and they said my brother and I were to go to the police station. When they brought us there, they put us in a room, where they beat us. They gave us a big ashtray which was full of cigarette butts, filters, and parts of cigarettes, together with the ash.
