They made us eat this. First one soldier put one or two cigarette butts into our mouths, and then they made us eat all of it. They beat us with police truncheons. They asked us to say at whose house we had hidden our cars. My brother was driving a new Mercedes at the time, and I was driving a new Honda; I mean, just before the war broke out. I told them that I had handed over our jeep to Mr. Lugar, who at that very moment appeared in the doorway. After this, Todorovic took my brother across the corridor into another room, as had happened the very first time we had been brought to the police station. Todorovic and a few other police officers beat him. And I was paralysed by fear, sitting with Lugar and an officer I didn't know who was sitting at the desk across from me. I heard quite clearly that they addressed him as "Grof" which means "Count." They gave us paper and pencils and told us to write down everything we knew. When we asked what we should write down, the policeman or soldier - he was wearing a camouflage uniform - who had made us eat the cigarette butts hit me on the head several times and told me to write down everything I knew. Through both open doors, I could see that something similar was happening to my brother, and this was being done to him by Todorovic. When I started writing, I received a blow on the hands with that same truncheon and was told to write in the Cyrillic alphabet, to be sure that I had learnt the Cyrillic alphabet in the first few years of primary school. But that was more than 25 years before, and I could no longer write in the Cyrillic alphabet. Then the gentleman whom they addressed as Grof asked Lugar whether it was true we had handed over our jeep, and Lugar confirmed this. He said yes. He asked where the vehicle was now. Lugar said, "It's in a safe place in Priboj."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did they let you go?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a certain time, the gentleman nicknamed Grof asked if there was room downstairs; he was referring to the cellars of the police station. One of the men who were moving around in the corridor said the basement was full. Then he gave orders that we be taken back to the primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, since we're going to get back to the primary school, I think it now would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We'll have our lunch break a little early and resume our proceedings at 1530 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution is continuing with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Could the usher please show the witness Exhibit 14A, photographs 68 and then 67. 68 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bicic. Do you see the person depicted in photograph number 68? Do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise him. That's Lugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you now look at photograph 67. Do you recognise that patch?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the insignia of the Sivi Vukovi, or Grey Wolves, or rather, the members of that Serb special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And did you see anyone in Bosanski Samac in April of 1992 wearing a patch like that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw it several times on these people, when I dared look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Could you place the diagram of the primary school back on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we leave the patch, the witness said he saw it several times on these people when he dared look at them. Whom? Whom does he mean? Who were "these people"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Which people are you talking about that you saw in Bosanski Samac wearing those patches?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people from the special forces, to which Lugar himself belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: The persons who were doing the beatings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I wanted to find out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: The persons who were doing the beatings, Mr. Bicic? Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Were they with a foreign accent, or were they locals?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were those the people from Serbia that you mentioned, or were those the local individuals from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning they were mostly people from Serbia who had the Ekavian accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: In photograph 68 that you identified as Lugar, is that the individual who you've been talking about yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us return to the primary school, end of June/early July 1992, approximately one week, or during the week just before your brother was transferred. Do you recall a situation or an incident, or several incidents, where you and the other prisoners were forced to beat each other?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. On one occasion, Todorovic and his escorts Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. entered the hall we were incarcerated in - that is to say, they came into the gym - and they ordered us to sing. Among others, there was a close relative of Todorovic's whose name was Goran Todorovic, with another man. His name was Rade. I don't know where he was from. After shouting out slogans such as "Serbia stretching to Tokyo" and the songs that we sang, he chose Rade, that is, selected several -- singled out several of us, whom he beat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, were the prisoners forced to beat each other at their request on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Could you explain who had to fight who and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They forced me and my brother and my friend Ibrahim Salkic to beat one another. And if we didn't beat one another hard enough, then they would beat us using different implements such as, for example, Rade used a rod or bar, a lightning rod, which was metal, a flat metal object. It was 3 or 4 centimetres wide and about 5 millimetres thick. And then he would force one of us to place his hands on his back, chest out as much as possible, and then he'd take that metal rod and strike blows across the chest. On that occasion when he took a swing to hit me, I moved. I ducked. And instead of getting one blow like all the others, he hit me three times with that same metal rod across the chest. Then he made us beat each other again. And during this situation, somebody - I can't say who, because it came from behind - hit me with a baseball bat on the head in the region of my nose, eye and nose, so that my nose was broken and the arch above the eye was slit open and bled profusely. They put toilet paper up my nose or handkerchiefs, which somebody happened to have on them, but this bleeding from the nose lasted for more than 20 days. Whenever I tried to take out the tampons, the blood would rush forward and it would start bleeding again. So from that time on to the present day, I find it very difficult to breathe through my nose. And all this part here was broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did something happen to your brother on that day? Did his hand get reinjured?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That day when they broke my bones, they allowed me to lie down on the floor, on this plastic floor covering of the gym. They then proceeded to beat my brother. Stevan Todorovic beat him, and I was able to watch this while I was lying on the floor. He beat him with a baseball bat. My brother placed his -- put his hands -- can I demonstrate this? He put his hands up to his head, and he broke the fingers again, the ones who had grown together, who knows how. They also beat Salkic and the other people, while Omer Nalic was standing in front of us somewhere in the middle of the room. And he was like a conductor. He conducted while the others had to sing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How many fingers were broken in your brother's hand?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that moment, three fingers were fractured on his left hand once again, the ones that had grown together. His hand was swollen a great deal. He was suffering a great deal of pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into a private session? I was going to talk to this -- interview this witness about two brief incidents. One is sexual in nature, and some of the detail could indicate who the persons were who had to commit certain acts. And also one is a kind of disgusting act, where he's going to mention the name. Less than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can go into private session actually. So there is no need to draw the blinds down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: You're aware that your brother was exchanged in early July, on July 4th, Mr. Bicic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about that day, what happened, how your brother came about to being exchanged that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, several policemen wearing policemen's uniforms came in with lists. They read out names from the list, called some people out who were on the list for the exchange, and among them was my brother. However, while those people were reading through the list, Rade and his entourage turned up again. And as I say, sometimes they would visit us twice a week. And when my brother's name was read out, they became very angry. They swore, said, "Who put him on the list for the exchange?" cursing and swearing all the time and insulting us. They started to beat him, him and the others whom they had called out. The policemen who were calling out the names, reading the names out, did not even try to stop them. Quite simply, they carried on reading out the names from the list, while these others kept beating and inflicting heavy blows with implements and boots, throwing the people out into the corridor, and all the others. I think that from that particular group, seven to ten people were exchanged. I can't say with certainty, but I think that that was roughly the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you get to speak to your brother before he left on that date?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we didn't even have a chance to say goodbye to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, after the prisoners leave - that's group of prisoners leave - to be exchanged, what happens?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a few days went by, some younger people came to the hall, some new people that we hadn't seen around before. They were now accompanying Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Actually, before that, Mr. Bicic, did Goran Todorovic or Rade do anything to the prisoners after that group was taken outside, to the remaining prisoners? Was there an incident where someone was used as a horse or called a horse?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the members of the Chamber what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, as they themselves said, they had seen them off nicely to the bus where they were put up - that means that they beat them the whole time - they returned with some more people in uniform. They went back to the hall, and they started beating everybody one by one. When my turn came, they beat me until I fell down. When I fell to the floor, Rade got up on my back and beat me with his baton on my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. head, with his police baton on my head, while two soldiers from his company went to the side to beat me in the area of my kidneys. They hurried me up. They wanted me to crawl on all fours, to get me down on all fours, crawling on my arms and legs, carrying Rade on my back in this way around the hall. After the second circle, from all the beating and my general exhaustion, I lost consciousness, so that I do not know what happened for some time after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What were you beaten with? Mr. Bicic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rade beat me, as I've already said, with a baton on my head, and forced me, screaming out that that was the way horses were driven, while the other two who held him up on my back -- they held him by the uniform that he had on him and kicked me with their boots, their army boots, in the kidneys, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you indicated a few days later some new people came. Have you ever heard of a man or do you recall a person by the name of Truman, using the nickname of Truman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who he was, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a young man, about 20 years old. His father was from the neighbouring village. Well, not actually neighbouring village but the village after Prud. For a time, he played football. He was a goalkeeper in the Odzak football club. And afterwards, I think he played in Brcko -- Slavonski Brod, or whatever the club's name was. However, we heard in the camp, when these new people turned up, that on the territory of Odzak, in the fighting there, this man Truman - that is to say, the father of this young guy - had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: The first time you saw this Truman, did someone bring him to visit the camp or did he come on his own?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first time he came together with -- or rather, he was one of the escorts of Stevan Todorovic. He came with a group of people who were also in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Todorovic showed Truman - this younger one, the young guy - he showed him how he should behave towards us, towards us prisoners, how to revenge the death of his father by -- actually, this event with his -- what had happened to his father, this incident, was nothing to do with us. None of us had anything to do with his father's death. So as I was saying, he showed him and his people how to do what they did, how to beat us, what to use to beat us with. He showed him very well that he was not to do it with his hands. He was to save his own hands and use different objects, because he said, "You will need your hands for something else. So use your legs, your boots." So that then again, we were, almost all of us, beaten in that hall. That went on for about an hour. They beat some of us, while others had to sing. Then they would put those people back -- take those people back and take others. They reversed the roles; now the others sang and the first lot were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Thereafter, did you ever see Truman again? Did he visit again after that date?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that day, he was also -- he became a frequent visitor of the hall we were locked up in, but mostly, as I say, mostly he personally would take out the prisoners of Croatian ethnicity. So he selected them mostly, the Croats. They were victims rather than us belonging to the Muslim ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What did he use to beat you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like all the others before him, he used different objects, rifles, his legs, boots. He used the scrap objects that I indicated earlier on and also the batons that he brought with him. They were wooden truncheons. Anything and everything that came to hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did he ever bring anyone with him, or did he come alone?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He always came with a group of people. He never came alone. Very rarely did any of them come alone, with the exception of these Serb special forces who beat us at the beginning. All the others would always come in larger groups at night, and they came with people who wore masks on their heads, which indicated to us that they might have been people from our own town, our former friends or perhaps neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Stjepanovic brothers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Do you recall Truman doing something to the Stjepanovic brothers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Like Rade, he put aside those two brothers and forced them to beat each other, just like they forced me and my brother to fight. Then he would beat them in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the beating of Andrija Stjepanovic with a bat?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. On that occasion, he beat Andrija Stjepanovic so hard with his bat, baton - I think it was a wooden baton - that he broke his nose. And when Andrija entreated him to kill him and not to torture him further because he couldn't take it any more, he beat a man called Jakov as well. He was incarcerated with us there too. He beat him so much -- what he did was he placed him by the wall, and then he would take a run at him from the middle of the hall. He would rush up to him and jump on his chest and kick him with his boots, and the man would fall down from the force of the blows, and then he would carry on kicking him. The other people would come to his assistance, the people who were around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall two soldiers or police officers named Zvaka and Zubar?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember a policeman called Zvaka and another policeman whom we nicknamed Zubar, meaning --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: It means "dentist"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a man - or rather, young guy. He was about 20 - who would take our teeth out with pliers, and that's why we nicknamed him Zubar, "the dentist."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Let's start out with Zvaka. How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zvaka was from around Samac. He worked in the department store not far from our pizzeria. He was also a frequent customer in our pizza bar, and during the day and in the evening ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. And what would happen during the day and in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to Zubar. Who is Zubar?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that he was a young man of about 20 who was in the police force, the Serb police. He would come on duty to guard us in the vehicle, and his father had German number plates on the car. He would -- that is to say, the younger people who were incarcerated with us often had to wash his car and maintain his car. And he would take out a harmonica, which he played very badly, very, very badly - he would just strike a few notes - whereas all the rest of us had to sing, and while we were singing, he was playing in the corridor. He ordered us to sing louder, to sing different songs, so that -- this accordian, actually, was worse than the beatings, and this went on in all the shifts, whenever he was on duty, whenever he was the guard on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: The songs that he made you sing, were these Chetnik songs or Serbian patriotic songs as he played his accordion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were Chetnik songs. But he didn't know how to play them on his accordion. He just opened and shut it, stretched it, and made some kind of rhythm which he alone could recognise, and that got on our nerves and made our ears tingle. But we had to sing. We had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall Zvaka and Zubar doing something one evening in August? Do you recall that incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. One evening - I don't know what time it was, but it was dark - people came into the hall. There was a lot of noise. They forced us to sing again, and while we were singing, a few of them would just catch hold of one by one of us and throw us out into the corridor, in front of the hall. Then others would get hold of us there, who would then hold us by -- hold our arms and twist our arms round to the back of our -- to the back, to our backs. One of them would then start jumping up with his knees into our backs and catch hold of our heads, and when we opened our mouths, they would shove an object into our mouths so that we were unable to shut our mouths. Zubar came to their assistance then and then used pliers to extract people's teeth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were these new pliers or sanitary pliers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were pliers that had perhaps once upon a time been used for medical purposes, but they weren't new, and they were all bloody, and I thought they were rusty too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were any of your teeth pulled on that evening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I lost two teeth that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Do you know any other prisoners who lost teeth on that evening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Dragan Delic, who was the director of an enterprise in Samac before the war - it was called Mebos - they pulled six of his teeth. Safet Hadzialijagic, who was the head of the waterworks department, lost four or five teeth. They pulled four or five of his teeth out. Then there was Dasa, Mersad Gibic. The same thing happened to him, and to Avdo Drljacic. There were very few of us who were left in the gym hall whose teeth they did not pull out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: How many teeth were extracted on that evening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning when we swept the place - that is to say, the younger guys would usually clean up the floor - they said that there were over 100 teeth lying around in the corridors and hallways. Later on, when I was transferred to the Territorial Defence building again, they told me, the people there told me that they had visits too by those same people and that they pulled out teeth there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, using the diagram, can you show the Court where the teeth were extracted on that evening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in this area here, the main corridor in front of the entrance to the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just quickly, Mr. Bicic, I'm going to take you to your last interrogation sometime in mid to late July by a Simo Bovic [sic]? Do you know a man by the name of Simo Bovic [sic]? Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Simo Bozic. Before the war, he worked for several years as a magistrate in our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And did he have a certain job or role with the municipality in dealing with the prisoners, interrogating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which role he had at the time, but one day, he came that is to say, Dzoko Maslic came, who had worked in the police force before the war as a police technician. I don't know in what department. But he came into the hall to fetch me. He put me into a car and drove me to the gym hall of the secondary school centre, and from there he brought Zlatan Avramovic, who was also a young man from Samac. While I was sitting in the car waiting for him to bring Zlatan Avramovic out, a guard who was standing outside said through the open window -- there was a broken window, or it couldn't be shut - I don't know - a window of the car. He didn't say. He hit me with the butt of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. his rifle in the head; luckily for me, not very hard. Dzoko came back with Zlatan and made the soldier leave. He drove us to the police station and handed me over to Simo Bozic, to whom I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And how long were you with Simo Bozic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the office that Simo Bozic was in, I spent about half an hour in that office. Then I waited outside in the hallway for Zlatan Avramovic to go through the same proceedings. When Zlatan was finished with making the statement - and he spent about an hour there too - we waited for somebody to come and take us back to -- me to the primary school building, and Zlatan was taken to the secondary school centre. Zubar came up to us again, who happened to be passing by, and as I was turned -- as I had my back turned, he hit me with his rifle butt in the back. I screamed out because it hurt a lot. Simo Bozic came out of his office, made Zubar leave. He called Dzoko Maslic again, who took me back to the primary school together with Zlatan, whom he first deposited at the secondary school gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, your statement to Simo Bozic, did you get to read it after you completed the statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Even if I did, I don't know what purpose it would have served, because if I had been beaten before that and if I was beaten after that, then what was the purpose of the statement? They could have given me my death sentence to sign, and it wouldn't have been much worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: During the interview with Simo Bozic, were you treated fairly or were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During the interrogation, nobody beat me. I was interviewed by Mr. Bozic. I answered his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: So you were returned to the primary school after the interview?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Now, sometime in late August, were you moved to another facility?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before they transferred us back to the warehouse of the Territorial Defence, an incident took place so that a group of -- what happened was that a group of people came in to where we were. They singled out some of us as their victims. They beat us, but at that particular moment especially -- they especially singled out Mr. Safet Hadzialijagic, nicknamed Coner. They beat him. Four or five of them beat him, put him in a circle that they had formed around him, while the rest of us, as had happened in all the previous cases, had to stand around singing the Chetnik songs. They beat him so much that when he fell down, they struck him with their boots, kicking him in the head. And in one particular instance, after having kicked him, there was blood on the boot of one of the soldiers. He was swearing and cursing his balija mother at Safet. He said why had Safet dirtied his boot with his blood. And he swore at him for that and then made Safet lick his boot clean and lick his blood off the floor. The man screamed out in pain. To all of us, this was horrendous and caused us a great deal of pain to have to look at this helpless man. And we were helpless ourselves, exhausted with the daily beatings and the hunger. And at that time, we were given a piece of bread the size of a packet of cigarettes, stale bread several days old with half a spoonful of marmalade jam or half a spoonful of pork fat, lard, and about half a cup of tea. That was a meal which would have to keep us going for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, who were those persons who beat Safet Hadzialijagic? Were those locals? Were those soldiers? Were those police officers? Who was that group?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Safet Hadzialijagic was beaten by policemen. Some of them were local people, some from the Samac area. And in that beating and the extraction of teeth, the most prominent role was played by Nikola Vukovic. He arrived in Samac, shortly before the war broke out, from the Vukovar area. His wife was from Samac. Several years before that, she had been employed as an assistant cook in our restaurant which we had in the same place that we later refurbished and transformed into a pizzaria. The names of the others who took part were Zvaka, Tubonja, and some others whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Just a few more questions on the primary school. For those three months, let's say 12 to 14 weeks, that you spent in the primary school, were you allowed to bathe?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not once did we have an opportunity to bathe or to wash ourselves. If we went to the toilet to relieve ourselves or to wash, we first had to pass by the guards, and very often we did not know whose shift it was or whether they would allow us to go, or perhaps say they allowed us to go and then give us a beating in that corridor. I only wish to add one more thing: I think that this was happening all over town and not just in the school where we were locked up. There were only a few hours when the water was turned on; in other words, the town water supply was on for only a few hours, and then we would fill some containers which had been brought to us by the guards or policemen. We filled them with water in order to have drinking water, and if we were beaten again, the guards and those who beat us wanted us to be able to wash the floor of the detention room or to wipe the corridor in which we were most frequently beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: When you were transferred to the TO, where were you held at the TO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were transferred to the TO, we were accommodated in this other room. I would like to show this on the diagram, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do we have the TO diagram?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were brought back to the premises of the Territorial Defence, we were put in this larger storeroom, and in these rooms - there were two rooms, in fact - we found about a hundred people. I'm referring to the room where we had been detained before and the room next to it. There were about 100 or 120 people. I say approximately, because I didn't count them, nor would I have been able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Were prisoners beaten upon return at the TO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did Rade ever come and visit at the TO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rade continued his visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: And what happened when he visited?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, he would --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather -- sorry, interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he arrived, he would call out people's names. He would ask for the brothers Radic, for Jakov. And as the guards guarding us in those two rooms - and by that time we were also allowed to go out into the yard - they opened the doors, so we were able to move around the yard, sit outside. The guards were here, in the room here, in this building. They would come in - I don't know on that pretext - and they would come to where we were, call out Jakov and the Stjepanovic brothers. They would stand here near the door so that the guards could see them, and they would make these three men run from somewhere in the centre of the room and bang their heads against the walls. They would repeat this several times, until somebody from outside called the guards who were there. The guards would come quickly and throw them out, two or three times. However, they would have to bang their heads against the wall and they would faint from this effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, how long were you at the TO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the TO until the 4th of September, 1992, or rather, until the 3rd of September, 1992, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What happened on the evening of the 3rd of September?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening of the 3rd of September, several policemen came with lists. They called people out from those two rooms in which we were detained. Among others, they called me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then they took us out, put us onto a truck, where we sat in the darkness, waiting. And then they took several prisoners out of the police station and put them onto the same truck, and then they drove off. The truck was covered with canvas. The drive may have taken an hour or longer. It's difficult for me to orientate myself or to remember how long it took. And in the end, they brought us back to the primary school gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: What did you observe when you arrived at the primary school gymnasium?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the primary school gymnasium, there were many elderly people from our town and the surrounding area. Some of them were even over 80. These people were sitting on the floor. I knew many of them. When they saw me coming in with the guards who brought us in, who were carrying flashlights and candles, many of these people from our town got up. They simply jumped to their feet. They approached me, hugged me, gave me a cigarette, or a pack of cigarettes. They were happy to see me. They said that at last I too was to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: The next day, September 4th, can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, at about 8.00, these elderly civilians were brought in. They had a watch, and we knew then what time it was. Some buses arrived. I think there were two buses. They came to a halt in the yard outside the entrance facing the stairs leading into the gym. And then we waited for some other people, some women and children they had sent for. They were searching for them in the houses where they were staying. Then they started calling out names, and if someone's name was called out, he was told to board a bus. I was among those whose names were called out. I boarded a bus. Sometime after the buses had arrived on the -- the school playground or yard was full of people from our town. I don't know how they had found out, whether someone had told them, but they had simply gathered there to see us off. And so after about an hour, we set out, and then we stopped again in front of the police station building. A man was carried in from the police station. He had been wounded. I didn't know him. They also put him in the bus, and then the bus set off in the direction of Bosanska Gradiska. We arrived there between 1200 and 1300 hours. It was daylight. It was a very, very hot day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you see any of the defendants --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: Did you see any of the defendants when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The bus was in front of a bridge at a distance of 20 to 25 metres. I can't remember exactly. It was in a street. And on the opposite side of the street from the bus, some 10 or 15 metres away, there was a catering establishment, where I saw Mr. Miro Tadic together with some other policemen, some of whom I knew. They were drinking beer while we sat in the bus with the door and windows closed, in the burning sunshine. Some elderly women who had to go to the toilet had to relieve themselves sitting there in their clothes. And we stood there for about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. five hours waiting, then some other buses arrive. We didn't know where they were coming from. And shortly after this, we crossed the bridge and went on towards Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like to break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall rise now. Next week, Monday we're not sitting. On Tuesday, we're not sure whether we will have the courtroom, but we shall definitely have the courtroom in the afternoon at 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Should we consult the Registrar's office on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. On Monday we won't sit because the courtroom will be used the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, I realise that. Shall we consult the Registrar's office about the Tuesday, whether or not we'll be meeting in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Or is it definitely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll sit at 1500 hours on Tuesday.
